contentBlocks.text: Build WhatsApp-style messaging: follow the complete user journey

Read in order: each decision below follows from the same real-world situation. Domains ending in .example are reserved teaching names, not live services. These are illustrative designs, not descriptions of a company’s internal implementation.
1. Start with Alice and Bob, not a broker

Alice types “Meet at 6” and presses Send. Bob has no mobile connection. Alice should learn that the service accepted the message, while Bob must receive it after reconnecting. Accepted, delivered and read are different facts. We will build that sequence first. A live socket alone cannot satisfy it because disconnecting would lose the only delivery path.
2. How the apps find the service

The operator configures an owned hostname such as chat.learn.example in DNS, binds it to an HTTPS/WebSocket edge and provisions its certificate. The app has this approved service origin in configuration. The domain of Bob’s email address does not decide which server owns the chat. DNS locates the service; conversation and recipient IDs select application records after connection. A mobile reconnect can reach another server, so required state must not exist only on the old socket node.
3. Log in and send one message

Alice authenticates and establishes an authorized connection. A WebSocket handshake must validate the credential and permitted browser origins where applicable; being connected is not permission to post to every conversation. Alice sends {conversationId: c7, clientMessageId: m81, ciphertext: ...}. The service derives the sender from the session, verifies membership and checks that m81 has not already been accepted for that sender/conversation.
The concrete API/data vocabulary used in this journey:
POST /conversations/{id}/messages; GET messages?after=cursor. Message(conversation, sequence, sender, client_message_id unique within its scope, ciphertext). DeviceCursor tracks delivery.
A concrete request and observable response for this journey (illustrative API contract):
WhatsApp-style messaging component overview
Use this diagram to locate the responsibilities just introduced. Arrows show selected requests/data; the paragraphs distinguish return responses, alternatives and transaction boundaries.
4. Commit before showing accepted

Within the chosen database boundary, insert the message, assign its conversation sequence and store a delivery outbox event. Return accepted only after the promised durability level is met. If the response disappears, Alice retries m81 and receives the original sequence rather than creating another message. A single partition owner or transactional sequencer can order one conversation; phone clocks cannot reliably do so. An outbox relay can publish twice, so workers and recipients must tolerate duplicates.
5. Deliver now or recover later

A delivery worker looks up Bob’s connected devices in a session directory. When Bob is offline, a notification can wake his app but is not the message database. On reconnect Bob authenticates, proves membership again and requests messages after cursor 40. If he gets 42 before 41, he fetches the missing range. Devices deduplicate IDs, acknowledge delivered state and later explicitly report read state. History retention and tombstones determine what an old cursor can recover.
6. Keep privacy rules on every path

Check membership for send, history reads, attachment access and socket subscriptions, not just conversation creation. Revocation must reach live sessions or be enforced at each operation. End-to-end encryption happens on authorized devices using an established protocol; TLS alone only encrypts the connection to the service. Store encrypted envelopes and explicit metadata. Multi-device keys, attachments, backup recovery and joining/leaving groups require deliberate policies.
7. Rehearse the failures

Kill the socket server after database commit: the message remains and reconnect recovers it. Kill the worker after push: redelivery is possible and Bob deduplicates. Lose database access: do not acknowledge durable acceptance. Lose the membership service: deny protected reads/sends temporarily rather than bypass membership. Expire a device session: require reauthentication. For groups, choose a fan-out model that does not block acceptance on every recipient; huge groups may fetch shared history. Measure accepted-message latency, reconnect gaps and delivery lag separately.
8. Prove the first version before scaling

Begin with one authenticated API/socket service and durable conversation storage. Test two devices, an offline recipient, retry of the same client ID, forbidden conversation reads and history after reconnect. Then add multiple connection nodes, a shared session directory and background delivery workers for measured connection count and fan-out needs. Do not claim global ordering or exactly-once external effects merely because a broker exists.
Work the capacity assumption

100,000 connected users sending one message/minute produce about 1,667 sends/second before group fan-out and multi-device copies. These are illustrative assumptions; measure the chosen implementation and peak distribution before treating them as capacity.
Explain the journey back

How does Bob recover if he receives sequence 42 before sequence 41? Then explain the hostname, caller identity, object-level permission, authoritative record, success acknowledgement and crash/retry behavior for this same action.

question: How do you handle ordering and duplicates in chat?
answer: Network delays and retries can reorder or duplicate messages.
explanation: Retries and reconnects can duplicate or reorder delivery. Use a stable client message ID for deduplication and an authoritative per-conversation sequence for accepted order.
why: Numbered pages stay readable when the printer hands you the same page twice.
example: m81 gets sequence 41 but Alice loses the response. Retrying must return 41. Bob receiving 42 before 41 can detect a gap and fetch missing history.
tradeoffs: Conversation order is not global order. Huge groups can overload one ordering owner. Tombstones distinguish intentional deletion from a delivery gap.
followups: What about edits and deletes?

question: How would you design WhatsApp group messaging and presence?
answer: Fan-out cost grows with group size, and presence updates are ephemeral.
explanation: Fan-out-on-write prepares individual deliveries; fan-out-on-read fetches shared history. Presence is usually approximate, based on heartbeats and expiry rather than a guaranteed disconnect notification.
why: A group announcement has many recipients; an attendance light is only a recent hint.
example: A 50-member study group can use per-member delivery tasks. A 100,000-member announcement channel may prefer shared history and cursor reads.
tradeoffs: Joining/leaving affects history access and in-flight delivery. Each device needs a cursor. Broadcasting every presence change to a huge group can dominate load.

question: How does end-to-end encryption change messaging architecture?
answer: The server transports ciphertext but should not possess plaintext decryption keys.
explanation: End-to-end encryption keeps content encryption/decryption on endpoint devices. TLS protects a connection to the server but can still expose plaintext at that server. Use established audited protocols.
why: The server carries a locked parcel; only authorized devices can open it.
example: Alice encrypts for Bob’s authorized devices before upload. The server queues ciphertext for offline delivery and cannot directly run plaintext search over it.
tradeoffs: Server-side moderation and search change. Reports can deliberately disclose selected messages. Weak backups and compromised endpoints can defeat confidentiality.
followups: How do you handle key rotation and new devices?

question: Design an e-commerce platform from catalog to checkout.
answer: Catalog, search, cart, inventory, orders and payments have different scaling and consistency needs.
explanation: Catalog, cart, checkout, payment and fulfillment have different correctness needs. A cart records intent, not a permanent promise of price or availability.
why: Browsing uses a catalog copy; buying the last item needs the real stock ledger.
example: A buyer adds two mugs. One sells out and the price changes before checkout. The server must recompute current terms rather than trust browser totals.
tradeoffs: Long synchronous chains increase timeout exposure. A modular monolith is a useful starting point; separate services when ownership or scaling justifies them.
followups: How do you prevent overselling?

walkthroughSteps.explanation: Store item IDs and quantities under the authenticated customer; validate limits and ownership.

walkthroughSteps.explanation: Recompute authoritative price, reserve inventory and create an idempotent pending order.

contentBlocks.text: Build E-commerce checkout: follow the complete user journey

Read in order: each decision below follows from the same real-world situation. Domains ending in .example are reserved teaching names, not live services. These are illustrative designs, not descriptions of a company’s internal implementation.
1. Follow one purchase of the last mug

Alice adds mug-42 to her cart, then clicks Pay. At the same moment Bob buys the last available mug. Our task is to produce one correct order and one intended payment effect per purchase, while giving the losing buyer an honest sold-out result. Cached product pages are discovery views, not inventory reservations. Start by choosing where the stock decision is authoritative.
2. Where the browser sends requests

The shop operator owns shop.learn.example and configures DNS, edge routing and TLS for the web/API origin. A separate payment provider owns its own API/domain. The shop calls that approved provider endpoint from trusted configuration. A return URL shown to a browser is not proof of payment; a customer can visit or modify a browser URL. Confirm outcomes using authenticated server-to-server responses, signed callbacks and reconciliation.
3. Create a trusted checkout request

Alice signs in or receives a deliberately scoped guest-checkout session. POST /checkout contains item IDs, quantities, delivery choices and an idempotency key purchase-81, not a trusted total or owner ID. The server derives cart ownership from the verified session and recomputes price, currency, tax and eligibility. Cookie-based writes need CSRF protection. Card details should use the provider’s appropriate hosted/tokenized integration rather than passing raw card data through an interview toy API.
The concrete API/data vocabulary used in this journey:
POST /checkout with idempotency key. Order, OrderLine, Reservation(state, expiry), PaymentAttempt(provider key/status), Outbox. Calculate price on the server.
A concrete request and observable response for this journey (illustrative API contract):

POST /checkout
Authorization: Bearer <buyer-access-token>
Idempotency-Key: purchase-81
Content-Type: application/json

{"items":[{"sku":"mug-42","quantity":1}],"paymentMethodRef":"<provider-token>"}

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
{"orderId":81,"state":"PAYMENT_PENDING","statusUrl":"/orders/81"}

GET /orders/81
Authorization: Bearer <same-buyers-access-token>

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"orderId":81,"state":"CONFIRMED"}
E-commerce checkout component overview
Use this diagram to locate the responsibilities just introduced. Arrows show selected requests/data; the paragraphs distinguish return responses, alternatives and transaction boundaries.
4. Make the stock decision atomic

Inside a short local transaction, claim the purchase key, conditionally decrement available stock and create a pending order, reservation and payment outbox intent. UPDATE inventory SET available=available-1 WHERE sku=:sku AND available>=1 RETURNING available lets one buyer win the last unit. Check the affected row; an earlier SELECT is not a guarantee. If any required change fails, roll back all local changes. Do not hold this transaction open while a remote payment call runs.
5. Move from pending to a known payment result

A worker reads the committed intent and calls the provider with a stable provider idempotency key. A timeout means unknown: the card may already be charged. Query/retry using the same reference according to the provider contract. Verify webhook authenticity and deduplicate its event ID. A guarded order transition marks payment confirmed and records fulfillment intent. A duplicated callback cannot create a second shipment. A local transaction cannot magically include the remote provider.
6. Handle cancellation, expiry and refunds

Reserve stock for a defined interval. Expiry and payment success can race, so reservation states and version guards must decide exactly which action wins. A late successful charge after release needs policy: reacquire stock or refund. Refund is compensation recorded as a new business event, not rollback of time. Customers can only view/cancel their own orders; staff refund permissions and audit trails are separate from ordinary customer rights.
7. Search and browse without weakening checkout

Product changes flow to a derived search index; search can filter/rank and recommendations can fail independently. Cart entries carry item identity/quantity, not permanent price promises. A stale search result may show a sold-out mug; checkout revalidates authoritative state. Begin with transactional order/stock ownership, then split services only with a defined reservation protocol and recovery for partial success.
8. Test what the buyer sees under failure

Retry purchase-81 after losing its response and assert one order. Race two buyers for stock=1 and assert only one reservation. Delay payment success until after expiry and verify compensation. Submit someone else’s order ID and deny it. Simulate database outage before commit: do not report success. Stop analytics/email workers: the paid order remains durable. Track pending-payment age, reservation leaks, reconciliation backlog and duplicate-effect attempts, not only HTTP 200 counts.
Work the capacity assumption

For 60,000 checkouts/hour, average is 16.7/second. Flash-sale concentration on a single SKU may matter more than total average. These are illustrative assumptions; measure the chosen implementation and peak distribution before treating them as capacity.
Explain the journey back

Which local records must commit together to stop an order existing without a recoverable payment request? Then explain the hostname, caller identity, object-level permission, authoritative record, success acknowledgement and crash/retry behavior for this same action.

question: How do you prevent overselling during a flash sale?
answer: Inventory must never become negative even under concurrency.
explanation: A separate read of available=1 followed by a write lets competing buyers both decide to sell. Reserve with an atomic condition or equivalent serialization at the authoritative data boundary.
why: Two cashiers must not both promise the same last mug.
example: Buyers A and B request the final unit. A guarded database update lets only one committed transaction decrement available from 1 to 0.
tradeoffs: Hot rows serialize and create waiting. Keep transactions short and cap admission. Never hold the stock row lock while calling a payment provider.
followups: How do you expire abandoned reservations?

question: How do you design a reliable checkout and payment workflow?
answer: Payments are externally managed and cannot participate in one database transaction.
explanation: A saga records workflow progress across local transactions and external effects. A compensation is a new action such as refunding a charge; it does not erase history.
why: Stock reservation and card payment are separate promises; a timeout undoes neither.
example: A provider charges the card but its response times out. Keep the result unknown/pending and reconcile using the original provider key; a fresh key can double-charge.
tradeoffs: Callbacks may be delayed, duplicated or out of order. A success after stock expiry requires a policy such as reacquisition or refund.
followups: How do you reconcile PSP and local ledger?

walkthroughSteps.title: Record intent
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Commit pending order, reservation and payment-request outbox event together when they share a database.

walkthroughSteps.title: Request payment
walkthroughSteps.explanation: A worker calls the provider with a stable idempotency key outside the database transaction.

walkthroughSteps.title: Verify outcome
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Authenticate callbacks, deduplicate provider event IDs and query the provider for unknown outcomes.

walkthroughSteps.title: Transition once
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Guard order-state changes; confirm and fulfill, or release/refund according to recorded outcome and policy.

knowledgeCheck: Why is unknown more accurate than failed after a payment timeout?
diagram: Record intent → Request payment → Verify outcome → Transition once

lessonSections.title: Create a trusted checkout request
lessonSections.explanation: Alice signs in or receives a deliberately scoped guest-checkout session. POST /checkout contains item IDs, quantities, delivery choices and an idempotency key purchase-81, not a trusted total or owner ID. The server derives cart ownership from the verified session and recomputes price, currency, tax and eligibility. Cookie-based writes need CSRF protection. Card details should use the provider’s appropriate hosted/tokenized integration rather than passing raw card data through an interview toy API.

lessonSections.title: Make the stock decision atomic
lessonSections.explanation: Inside a short local transaction, claim the purchase key, conditionally decrement available stock and create a pending order, reservation and payment outbox intent. UPDATE inventory SET available=available-1 WHERE sku=:sku AND available>=1 RETURNING available lets one buyer win the last unit. Check the affected row; an earlier SELECT is not a guarantee. If any required change fails, roll back all local changes. Do not hold this transaction open while a remote payment call runs.

lessonSections.title: Move from pending to a known payment result
lessonSections.explanation: A worker reads the committed intent and calls the provider with a stable provider idempotency key. A timeout means unknown: the card may already be charged. Query/retry using the same reference according to the provider contract. Verify webhook authenticity and deduplicate its event ID. A guarded order transition marks payment confirmed and records fulfillment intent. A duplicated callback cannot create a second shipment. A local transaction cannot magically include the remote provider.

lessonSections.title: Handle cancellation, expiry and refunds
lessonSections.explanation: Reserve stock for a defined interval. Expiry and payment success can race, so reservation states and version guards must decide exactly which action wins. A late successful charge after release needs policy: reacquire stock or refund. Refund is compensation recorded as a new business event, not rollback of time. Customers can only view/cancel their own orders; staff refund permissions and audit trails are separate from ordinary customer rights.

lessonSections.title: Test what the buyer sees under failure
lessonSections.explanation: Retry purchase-81 after losing its response and assert one order. Race two buyers for stock=1 and assert only one reservation. Delay payment success until after expiry and verify compensation. Submit someone else’s order ID and deny it. Simulate database outage before commit: do not report success. Stop analytics/email workers: the paid order remains durable. Track pending-payment age, reservation leaks, reconciliation backlog and duplicate-effect attempts, not only HTTP 200 counts.

question: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
answer: Writing DB state and publishing an event separately can lose events.
explanation: Transactional outbox stores the business update and an event in one database transaction. A relay publishes committed rows later, closing the crash window between database commit and event publish.
why: Write the order and the instruction to announce it on the same durable page.
example: Order 81 becomes confirmed alongside outbox event e81. An API crash after commit cannot erase the event the relay must publish.
tradeoffs: Delivery is normally at least once, not automatic exactly once. Monitor oldest outbox age and preserve per-aggregate ordering when needed.
followups: Compare outbox polling with CDC.
learningTitle: Commit a business change and event together

walkthroughSteps.title: Commit both
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Update the order and insert e81 with event ID and aggregate version in one transaction.

walkthroughSteps.title: Relay committed rows
walkthroughSteps.explanation: A poller or change-data-capture reader publishes to the broker.

walkthroughSteps.title: Record publication progress
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Mark progress after broker acknowledgement; a crash before marking can republish.

walkthroughSteps.title: Deduplicate consumer
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Commit consumer effect and processed event ID atomically, or use an idempotent state transition.

question: Design product search, filtering and recommendations.
answer: Search requires full-text relevance and faceting beyond transactional joins.
explanation: Text search ranks matching documents; filters restrict exact attributes; recommendations rank candidates using context. Search indexes are derived and may lag behind authoritative catalog changes.
why: The shop directory finds a shelf; the cashier verifies the purchase terms.
example: Search running shoes with size 9 and relevance sorting. Recommendations suggest socks; checkout independently revalidates stock, price and eligibility.
tradeoffs: Provide a default ranking for new users and a fallback if recommendations fail. Monitor index lag; stable cursor pagination may suit changing results.
followups: How do you handle zero-result queries?
learningTitle: Design discovery as a derived view

walkthroughSteps.title: Change catalog
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Commit product attributes and a versioned source event.

walkthroughSteps.title: Update index
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Apply newer versions and tombstones idempotently; support rebuilding from history or snapshots.

walkthroughSteps.title: Search and rank
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Apply text query, filters, pagination and visibility rules before returning eligible candidates.

walkthroughSteps.title: Recheck purchase
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Use authoritative state for checkout instead of trusting the search copy.

knowledgeCheck: What should users still be able to do when recommendations are down?
diagram: Change catalog → Update index → Search and rank → Recheck purchase

lessonSections.explanation: Alice adds mug-42 to her cart, then clicks Pay. At the same moment Bob buys the last available mug. Our task is to produce one correct order and one intended payment effect per purchase, while giving the losing buyer an honest sold-out result. Cached product pages are discovery views, not inventory reservations. Start by choosing where the stock decision is authoritative.

lessonSections.explanation: Product changes flow to a derived search index; search can filter/rank and recommendations can fail independently. question: Design an Uber-like ride-hailing system.
answer: Match riders with nearby drivers in real time while tracking trip state and location updates.
explanation: Driver location is fast-changing and approximate. A confirmed assignment and trip lifecycle need stronger durable correctness. Separate these two kinds of state.
why: Dispatch finds candidates, offers a trip and allows exactly one valid assignment.
example: A rider requests pickup near a station. Nearby available drivers are shortlisted, ranked by pickup time and offered the ride with an acceptance deadline.
tradeoffs: Location can be stale or spoofed. Recheck availability when claiming, not just when searching. Reconnects recover durable trip state.
followups: How do you ensure only one driver accepts a ride?
learningTitle: Match a rider and run a trip

walkthroughSteps.title: Request ride
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Authenticate and create one pending trip under an idempotency key.

walkthroughSteps.title: Find candidates
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Read fresh nearby positions and estimate pickup times.

walkthroughSteps.title: Offer and claim
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Use bounded offers; acceptance must atomically prevent rider/driver double-assignment.

walkthroughSteps.title: Run lifecycle
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Persist accepted, arrived, started and completed states; publish updates and coordinate payment.

contentBlocks.text: Build Uber-style ride hailing: follow the complete user journey

Read in order: each decision below follows from the same real-world situation. Domains ending in .example are reserved teaching names, not live services. These are illustrative designs, not descriptions of a company’s internal implementation.
1. Follow a station pickup

Alice requests a car at a railway station. Driver D7 appears closest, but another rider is also trying to book D7. We need to find likely candidates quickly and then confirm exactly one valid assignment. Fresh-looking coordinates are a search hint; authoritative trip/driver state decides whether the assignment exists. A diagram that treats those as the same fact misses the core race.
2. How rider and driver apps connect

Both apps use the operator’s configured HTTPS origin, for example rides.learn.example, backed by owned DNS, edge bindings and TLS. Authenticated APIs carry durable requests; sockets or push carry timely updates. GPS selects a geographic search area inside the application, not a different DNS domain for every driver. Region routing can reduce latency, but ownership of a trip/driver must remain explicit during handoff.
3. Authenticate roles and validate a ride request

POST /rides includes pickup, destination, quote ID and an idempotency key. Derive rider identity from credentials. Validate supported area and quote terms. A driver session may update only its own authorized vehicle/location and accept offers addressed to that driver. Rider and driver permissions differ; guessing a trip ID must not reveal another passenger’s route or permit cancellation.
The concrete API/data vocabulary used in this journey:
POST /rides; POST /offers/{id}/accept with expected state/version. DriverPosition(timestamp, coordinates), Trip(state, rider, driver, version), Assignment.
A concrete request and observable response for this journey (illustrative API contract):
Uber-style ride hailing component overview
Use this diagram to locate the responsibilities just introduced. Arrows show selected requests/data; the paragraphs distinguish return responses, alternatives and transaction boundaries.
4. Find candidates then send expiring offers

Drivers publish timestamped positions. A geographic index searches the pickup cell plus neighbors, expanding radius if needed. Discard stale/ineligible candidates and compute road ETAs for a bounded shortlist: distance across a river can be misleading. Send offers containing trip, driver, expiry and expected state/version. Choosing one candidate is not yet a successful booking.
5. Confirm one driver with guarded state

On acceptance, recheck expiry and availability. If trip and driver share a database boundary, conditionally reserve the available driver and move the pending trip to accepted in one transaction, with an outbox update. Roll back if either condition fails. If separately owned shards/services are involved, use an assignment owner or recoverable reservation protocol with fencing. Do not pretend a short Redis lock supplies a cross-service transaction.
6. Run the trip and price contract

Persist allowed transitions: accepted, arrived, started, completed or a permitted cancellation. Late acceptances and old client versions cannot rewind state. A quote has stored currency, terms, pricing-policy version and expiry. ETA is a prediction based on route/traffic and should communicate uncertainty. Local demand/supply can inform bounded, smoothed surge policy; the rider accepts recorded terms rather than an undocumented moving price.
7. Recover when phones and workers fail

If Alice loses connection after assignment commit, a retry/reconnect fetches the same durable trip. Duplicate offers cannot assign D7 twice. An expired offer is rejected even if the phone shows it. If the position store fails, avoid inventing nearby drivers; use a documented temporary-unavailable policy. Stop status-push delivery: clients can refresh durable state. A payment timeout after trip completion requires separate payment reconciliation, not changing the trip back to started.
8. Build and verify in stages

First test one region with a few drivers, neighbor-cell search, two competing riders, late acceptance, stale coordinates and forbidden trip reads. Then measure position write volume, candidate-search time, assignment conflicts and notification lag. Add geographic partitioning for fleet size and load, while retaining a clear owner for assignments and tested recovery during region failure.
Work the capacity assumption

50,000 drivers updating every five seconds create 10,000 location writes/second; coalesce updates and expire old positions. These are illustrative assumptions; measure the chosen implementation and peak distribution before treating them as capacity.
Explain the journey back

Why might the nearest driver in straight-line distance not have the shortest pickup ETA? Then explain the hostname, caller identity, object-level permission, authoritative record, success acknowledgement and crash/retry behavior for this same action.

question: How do you find nearby drivers efficiently?
answer: Full scans of all driver coordinates are too slow.
explanation: Spatial indexes narrow coordinate searches without scanning the whole fleet. Cells, geohashes and spatial database indexes are options. Straight-line distance is only a candidate filter.
why: Search nearby map cells first, then compare actual road travel.
example: The closest driver is across a river. A slightly farther driver on the same side may reach the rider sooner.
tradeoffs: Small cells create many neighbor queries; large cells scan many drivers. GPS jitter and high update rates need thresholds and expiry.
followups: How do you update driver location without write overload?

walkthroughSteps.explanation: Store driver ID, coordinates, timestamp and availability hint; expire stale observations.

walkthroughSteps.title: Search neighboring cells
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Include boundary neighbors and expand the radius if there are too few candidates.

walkthroughSteps.title: Filter shortlist
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Reject stale, incompatible or unavailable drivers before expensive route calculations.

walkthroughSteps.title: Rank by travel ETA
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Compute route-based estimates for a bounded shortlist; matching still claims atomically.

question: How do you design trip state and matching concurrency?
answer: Trip lifecycle must prevent contradictory transitions.
explanation: A state machine lists allowed transitions. Compare-and-set or a transaction checks the expected state/version before writing. Lock expiry alone cannot prevent an old holder writing stale state.
why: Two dispatchers may propose the same driver, but only one claim should win.
example: Two riders compete for driver D7. In one database, a conditional transition from available to reserved can succeed for only one transaction.
tradeoffs: Separate shards cannot share a normal local transaction. Use an assignment owner or recoverable reservation protocol with fencing rather than assuming global atomicity.
followups: What happens when driver disconnects after acceptance?

walkthroughSteps.explanation: Identify pending trip T81 and driver D7; this snapshot does not guarantee later availability.

walkthroughSteps.title: Claim atomically
walkthroughSteps.explanation: In one local transaction when possible, claim the available driver and accept the pending trip; rollback if either condition fails.

walkthroughSteps.title: Publish after commit
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Commit an outbox event before telling clients the assignment is confirmed.

walkthroughSteps.title: Reject late actions
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Check expected state/version for acceptance or cancellation; return current state for stale requests.

question: How do surge pricing and ETA estimation work?
answer: Demand/supply imbalance influences dispatch and pricing, but models need guardrails.
explanation: ETA estimates travel from routes, traffic and pickup conditions. Surge responds to recent demand/supply under a defined pricing policy. Inputs need freshness, smoothing and fallback behavior.
why: An arrival time is a forecast; a quote has agreed terms and an expiry.
example: An illustrative area sees 100 requests and 20 available drivers in a recent window. That signal may inform pricing, but does not by itself define a trustworthy multiplier.
tradeoffs: Rapid feedback can cause oscillating prices. Define pricing and ETA fallback when data is unavailable and monitor prediction error.
followups: How do you test surge rules?
learningTitle: Distinguish an ETA from a price promise

walkthroughSteps.title: Collect signals
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Aggregate demand, supply and travel observations by area/window; detect stale inputs.

walkthroughSteps.title: Estimate pickup
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Route a shortlist and communicate uncertainty instead of a guaranteed arrival second.

walkthroughSteps.title: Store quote
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Apply a bounded, versioned policy and store quote ID, currency, terms and expiry.

walkthroughSteps.title: Bind accepted terms
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Accept an unexpired quote against its recorded terms; define any final-fare adjustment separately.
