question: How do virtual threads work, and when should you use them?
answer: Virtual threads are ordinary java.lang.Thread instances whose scheduling is managed by the JVM. A platform thread generally maps to an operating-system thread; many virtual threads share a smaller set of carrier platform threads. Java 21 finalized virtual threads (JEP 444). A Runnable describes work without a result; Callable describes work returning a result and allowing checked exceptions. Either task abstraction can run on a platform or virtual thread.
explanation: Virtual threads are ordinary java.lang.Thread instances whose scheduling is managed by the JVM. A platform thread generally maps to an operating-system thread; many virtual threads share a smaller set of carrier platform threads. Java 21 finalized virtual threads (JEP 444). A Runnable describes work without a result; Callable describes work returning a result and allowing checked exceptions. Either task abstraction can run on a platform or virtual thread. When supported blocking I/O parks a virtual thread, the JVM can unmount it from its carrier and later resume it on an available carrier. This lets many waiting tasks coexist without one OS thread per task. Concurrency means overlapping task lifetimes; parallelism means simultaneous CPU execution. Virtual threads improve throughput for many waiting tasks; they do not accelerate CPU computation or make a single remote call faster.
why: Use for high concurrency with blocking I/O. For CPU-heavy tasks use bounded parallelism near available processor capacity and measure. Compare throughput, p95/p99 latency, heap, carrier usage and downstream saturation under the same load.
example: For a service waiting on independent remote calls, a platform pool of 100 threads can become occupied by 100 waiting requests. Virtual threads allow more requests to wait cheaply, while a semaphore can still limit a remote service to four calls. The runnable demo submits 12 tasks, limits the simulated I/O section to four, releases permits in finally, checks isVirtual(), propagates failures and cancels outstanding tasks on error. It demonstrates scheduling/resource boundaries, not a performance benchmark.
tradeoffs: The virtual-thread-per-task executor is unbounded: one fresh virtual thread per submitted task. Do not pool virtual threads to control resources. Use a semaphore, connection pool, admission control and timeouts to bound downstream work; also bound incoming requests because waiting tasks still consume memory. Shared mutable state still requires synchronization. ThreadLocal works but large per-thread caches multiply memory use. Virtual threads are daemon threads; keep an owning scope alive and wait for completion. Cancellation is cooperative; configure real HTTP/JDBC timeouts because interruption may not stop every operation. On Java 21, blocking while holding a synchronized monitor can pin a carrier; long native/foreign calls can also occupy carriers. Diagnose with JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events and -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full on Java 21. JDK 24 (JEP 491) removes monitor-related pinning; do not repeat the Java 21 synchronized warning as a universal rule or replace every monitor with ReentrantLock. Lock contention and native-code limits still matter. Virtual threads need no preview flag in Java 21; other concurrency APIs have their own release status.
followups: Why does a virtual thread not remove the JDBC pool limit?
How do you bound incoming work as well as active downstream calls?
What is the difference between pinning on Java 21 and Java 24?
What happens when a Future times out but the remote call ignores interruption?
Why use a fixed platform pool for CPU-heavy computation?

question: Parking lot: levels, gates and atomic slot assignment?
answer: Design one parking-lot process that can admit vehicles through multiple entry gates and close tickets at exit gates without assigning the same slot twice.
explanation: Design one parking-lot process that can admit vehicles through multiple entry gates and close tickets at exit gates without assigning the same slot twice.
why: Start with the state and invariants, then choose classes, operations and synchronization.
example: A car enters E1 on level 1. There are car slots on levels 0 and 1 and a bike slot on level 0. Our explicit policy chooses an exact-type slot nearest the entry level, breaking ties by slot ID. The car receives ticket 1 for the level-1 slot; an exit gate later closes that ticket and returns the slot to the free pool.

lessonSections.title: Clarify the contract before classes
lessonSections.explanation: We model bike/car/truck kinds, numbered levels, entry/exit gates, active tickets and currently parked plates. This version uses exact-type fit; if motorcycles may occupy car spaces, introduce a documented compatibility rule. Full capacity returns no ticket. Duplicate active admission for the same plate and unknown/closed tickets are errors. Payment, pricing, reservation expiry and sensor reconciliation are extensions, not silently implemented features.

lessonSections.title: Assign responsibilities
lessonSections.explanation: Vehicle is immutable plate/type data. Slot has stable ID, level and kind. Gate has ID, level and direction. Ticket connects vehicle, assigned slot and entry gate. Lot owns the mutable free-slot and active-ticket indexes. Level is represented as a number on slots/gates; a richer product can promote it into a Level entity with physical capacity and display policies. UI panels and gate devices do not independently mutate the slot map.

lessonSections.title: Follow enter and exit
lessonSections.explanation: enter validates gate and vehicle, rejects an already parked plate, selects a free compatible slot, removes it from free state and records a ticket. All of those steps share one synchronized boundary. exit checks an exit gate and active ticket, removes the ticket/plate and releases that exact slot. A wrong-direction gate must fail before changing state. A repeated exit is rejected rather than incrementing availability twice.

lessonSections.title: Reason about concurrency and complexity
lessonSections.explanation: If two gates see one free slot, only one enter may finish with a ticket. The demo serializes the whole decision/update within one JVM. A free-slot scan costs O(s) for s available slots; indexes by level/type can improve selection but require consistent maintenance. Multiple application replicas need an authoritative database transaction/unique reservation or single assignment owner; synchronized does not coordinate separate processes.

lessonSections.title: Where authentication belongs
lessonSections.explanation: A real HTTP/gate integration authenticates devices/operators and authorizes permitted lot/gate actions outside this local object API. Knowing a ticket number should not permit arbitrary refunds or ticket edits. Persist ticket and occupancy changes transactionally if restart recovery is required. The demo deliberately keeps state in memory and does not claim durable parking control.

walkthroughSteps.title: Validate entry
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Check entry gate, vehicle kind and active plate before any slot mutation.

walkthroughSteps.title: Select a slot
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Choose exact kind, nearest entry level, then stable slot ID from the free pool.

walkthroughSteps.title: Commit admission
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Within the same lock, remove the slot and record vehicle plus ticket.

walkthroughSteps.title: Close through exit
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Validate exit gate and active ticket, then release exactly that slot once.

tradeoffs: The coarse lock favors correctness over throughput. Do not hold it while calling a payment terminal. A real payment/exit workflow needs recorded states and recovery for payment success followed by gate failure.
knowledgeCheck: How would you prevent two entry gates on different servers from assigning the last car slot?
diagram: Validate entry → Select a slot → Commit admission → Close through exit

question: Tic Tac Toe: model turns, legal moves and terminal states?
answer: Design a complete two-player 3×3 game using explicit board, player turn and game state. Choose Tic Tac Toe from the requested Chess-or-Tic-Tac-Toe exercise so the full rules can be implemented and tested.
explanation: Design a complete two-player 3×3 game using explicit board, player turn and game state. Choose Tic Tac Toe from the requested Chess-or-Tic-Tac-Toe exercise so the full rules can be implemented and tested.
why: Start with the state and invariants, then choose classes, operations and synchronization.
example: X places at (0,0). O cannot overwrite that cell, and X cannot immediately play again. Later X fills the top row and the game becomes X_WON. All subsequent moves must be rejected. A different nine-move sequence fills the board without a win and becomes DRAW.

lessonSections.title: Choose the objects and invariants
lessonSections.explanation: Mark is X or O; State is IN_PROGRESS, X_WON, O_WON or DRAW. Game owns a private 3×3 board, the current turn and the count of accepted moves. No UI or caller receives a mutable board reference. A move is accepted only when the game is active, the supplied player owns the turn, coordinates are in range and the cell is empty.

lessonSections.title: Execute one legal move
lessonSections.explanation: Validate before mutation, place the mark and increment move count. Check the affected row/column and both diagonals. A win takes precedence over draw on the final cell. If there is no win and all nine cells are filled, declare draw; otherwise switch the turn. A rejected move must not advance the turn or consume a move. This transition is synchronized in the lab.

lessonSections.title: Separate rules from interaction
lessonSections.explanation: A web controller translates an authorized player action into Game.move; a console or browser renders returned state. For online play, bind the authenticated user to an assigned mark server-side rather than accepting an arbitrary player field as authority. Persist moves or event history if reconnect/replay is required. A version guard can reject competing stale client moves across replicas.

lessonSections.title: Complexity and extension
lessonSections.explanation: For this fixed 3×3 board a move check has constant bounded work. A generalized n×n scan costs O(n) per move; row/column counters can reduce checking work when the rules allow it. Chess is a larger extension requiring piece-specific movement, obstruction, check/checkmate, castling and promotion; those are not provided by renaming this board. Avoid inheritance hierarchies with unused piece types for a game with only two marks.

lessonSections.title: Verify the rules, not only a happy path
lessonSections.explanation: The lab checks wrong turn, occupied cell, out-of-range coordinates, row and diagonal wins, draw and moves after termination. Add O wins, column/anti-diagonal wins and replay/version behavior when extending. Tests should assert that rejected commands leave state unchanged; they should not merely assert a status label after every method.

walkthroughSteps.title: Receive a player move
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Verify active game, assigned turn, coordinates and empty target cell.

walkthroughSteps.title: Apply once
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Place the mark and increase the count only after validation succeeds.

walkthroughSteps.title: Evaluate the board
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Check row, column and diagonals; win precedes draw.

walkthroughSteps.title: Transition state
walkthroughSteps.explanation: End on win/draw or switch the current turn; reject moves after termination.

tradeoffs: A local lock makes one Game instance atomic, not a shared online match across servers. A client-side win check is useful for display but the server must remain authoritative.
knowledgeCheck: Why must a full-board winning move become X_WON/O_WON rather than DRAW?
diagram: Receive a player move → Apply once → Evaluate the board → Transition state

question: LRU cache: expected O(1) lookup and eviction?
answer: Build a bounded least-recently-used cache. Successful get and updating an existing key make it most recent. When inserting beyond capacity, evict the least recent key.
explanation: Build a bounded least-recently-used cache. Successful get and updating an existing key make it most recent. When inserting beyond capacity, evict the least recent key.
why: Start with the state and invariants, then choose classes, operations and synchronization.
example: Capacity is two. put(1,A), put(2,B), get(1), put(3,C) must evict 2, because reading 1 made it newer. Updating 1 to A2 also refreshes it. A cache miss returns an explicit empty result; null keys/values are disallowed, and zero capacity is a disabled cache.

lessonSections.title: Why a map or list alone is insufficient
lessonSections.explanation: A hash map quickly locates a key but does not provide the eviction order. A list preserves order but searching the whole list is O(n). Combine HashMap<K,Node> with a doubly linked list so the map finds the exact node and the node links allow constant pointer updates. Head/tail sentinels simplify empty and single-element cases.

lessonSections.title: Write the invariants
lessonSections.explanation: Every map entry identifies exactly one list node. Every non-sentinel list node has a matching map entry. head.next is most recent and tail.prev is least recent. Forward/back links agree; size never exceeds capacity at the end of a public operation. Store only references internally; decide whether mutable cached values themselves require defensive copies at a higher boundary.

lessonSections.title: Trace get and put
lessonSections.explanation: get finds a node, detaches it and moves it to the head. A miss does not create an entry. put on an existing key updates the value and moves the same node. put on a new key creates a node and, if over capacity, detaches tail.prev and removes its key from the map. Eviction must update both structures, not only the list.

lessonSections.title: Explain the O(1) claim precisely
lessonSections.explanation: List unlink/link work is O(1). Hash-table operations are expected/amortized O(1) under normal hash distribution; do not claim deterministic constant time for every possible hash collision. Hash-map resizing can cost more for an individual operation. Memory is O(capacity). A successful get mutates recency, so it needs the same synchronization protection as writes in this exact-LRU implementation.

lessonSections.title: Compare implementation choices
lessonSections.explanation: Java LinkedHashMap with access-order configuration and an eviction hook is a concise alternative; the explicit node implementation demonstrates the underlying design. The lab uses synchronized public operations for exact local order. High-throughput caches often use more elaborate or approximate policies. LRU is an eviction rule, not TTL, persistence, freshness, authorization or a distributed consistency guarantee.

walkthroughSteps.title: Find the node
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Use the map to locate a key, returning empty on a miss.

walkthroughSteps.title: Refresh recency
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Detach the found/updated node and insert it immediately after the head.

walkthroughSteps.title: Enforce capacity
walkthroughSteps.explanation: On new insert beyond capacity, remove tail.prev from both list and map.

walkthroughSteps.title: Check structural safety
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Map/list membership and links must agree after every completed operation.

tradeoffs: Independent synchronization of map and list leaves races. A cached permission or price can still be stale. Decide cache validity separately from which entry is evicted.
knowledgeCheck: Why is get a write operation from the point of view of concurrency in an access-ordered LRU cache?
diagram: Find the node → Refresh recency → Enforce capacity → Check structural safety

question: Thread-safe HashMap: define atomic operations first?
answer: Design a map whose documented single-key operations are safe under concurrent access, then explain which compound operations still need one atomic boundary. Use a fixed striped teaching implementation, not a claim to reimplement ConcurrentHashMap.
explanation: Design a map whose documented single-key operations are safe under concurrent access, then explain which compound operations still need one atomic boundary. Use a fixed striped teaching implementation, not a claim to reimplement ConcurrentHashMap.
why: Start with the state and invariants, then choose classes, operations and synchronization.
example: Eight threads each increment count 1,000 times. The result must be 8,000. A thread-safe get followed by a thread-safe put can still lose increments because the combined read-modify-write was not atomic. compute holds one key’s bucket write lock across the update.

lessonSections.title: Start with the contract
lessonSections.explanation: Disallow null keys and values, use equals to distinguish colliding keys, define get-miss as null, allow compute returning null to remove a key, and provide an immutable consistent snapshot. Keys must keep stable hashCode/equals while stored. Thread-safe container structure does not make a mutable value object automatically safe.

lessonSections.title: Partition synchronization
lessonSections.explanation: Choose a fixed number of buckets. Each owns an ordinary HashMap and a read/write lock. Hash the key with floorMod to safely handle negative hashes including Integer.MIN_VALUE. Reads take a bucket read lock; puts and compute take its write lock. Operations in different buckets can proceed independently, while colliding keys intentionally contend on one bucket.

lessonSections.title: Make read-modify-write atomic
lessonSections.explanation: compute acquires the bucket write lock, reads old value, calculates replacement and updates/removes before unlocking in finally. Keep callbacks short, nonblocking and free of calls back into this map; calling across buckets or requesting a snapshot inside a callback can deadlock. An application needing external I/O should design that operation outside the lock with explicit race semantics.

lessonSections.title: Define global operations honestly
lessonSections.explanation: A snapshot acquires all bucket read locks in a fixed order and releases in reverse, copying values into an immutable map. That blocks writers and is O(number of entries + stripes), unlike the expected single-key lookup cost. Per-bucket HashMap resizing is protected by that bucket lock; this demo does not dynamically change the stripe array or offer lock-free reads.

lessonSections.title: Production comparison
lessonSections.explanation: Prefer Java ConcurrentHashMap when its documented operations match the need; use compute, merge or putIfAbsent instead of assuming get-plus-put is atomic. Do not describe modern ConcurrentHashMap as merely the old fixed Segment design. Its iteration/aggregate semantics differ from this lab’s all-bucket snapshot. A distributed key-value store additionally needs network, durability, replication and partition behavior.

walkthroughSteps.title: Select a bucket
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Use a stable key hash and floorMod; colliding keys still require equals checks.

walkthroughSteps.title: Acquire correct lock
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Read for get, write for put/compute; always release in finally.

walkthroughSteps.title: Complete one atomic change
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Read old value and write/remove the replacement within the same bucket lock.

walkthroughSteps.title: Coordinate a snapshot
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Acquire all bucket read locks in fixed order to make a consistent copied view.

tradeoffs: Stripes improve parallelism only for keys spread across buckets. Hot keys remain contended. This in-memory map has no restart recovery and coordinates no separate processes.
knowledgeCheck: Why can individually thread-safe get and put methods still produce a wrong concurrent counter?
diagram: Select a bucket → Acquire correct lock → Complete one atomic change → Coordinate a snapshot

question: Rate limiter: token-bucket LLD and distributed boundary?
answer: Implement a token bucket with injected time, atomic token accounting and tenant selection; then connect it to a cluster-wide admission design. The runnable Java bucket is local to one process.
explanation: Implement a token bucket with injected time, atomic token accounting and tenant selection; then connect it to a cluster-wide admission design. The runnable Java bucket is local to one process.
why: Start with the state and invariants, then choose classes, operations and synchronization.
example: A tenant starts with capacity 2 and refill 1 token/second. Two requests succeed immediately, the third is rejected. After half a second there is still no full token; after another half second one request succeeds. Fifty simultaneous requests against a frozen ten-token bucket admit exactly ten.

lessonSections.title: Define policy and objects
lessonSections.explanation: Bucket owns capacity, refill rate, tokens, last-observed time and a monotonic clock supplier. Limiter holds a fixed registry of configured tenant buckets so arbitrary keys cannot grow memory without bound in this demo. Each positive request cost consumes that many tokens; a cost above available tokens is rejected. Unknown tenants are rejected. Identity must already have been authenticated by the caller boundary.

lessonSections.title: Refill and consume atomically
lessonSections.explanation: Inside one synchronized operation, compute elapsed monotonic time, add elapsed*rate capped at capacity, then compare and subtract cost. Keep fractional tokens so half-second waits accumulate correctly. The lab injects an AtomicLong clock to test without sleeps. System.nanoTime is appropriate for local elapsed time; separate machines do not share a comparable nanoTime origin.

lessonSections.title: Connect to API behavior
lessonSections.explanation: On allow, continue to the backend, which still checks object-level authorization and resource capacity. On deny, return an appropriate HTTP 429 contract with retry guidance. Do not hold the bucket lock across backend processing. Rate limits bound arrivals; they do not replace in-flight limits, bounded queues, timeouts or backpressure.

lessonSections.title: Make cluster-wide semantics explicit
lessonSections.explanation: Deploying this Java map on five independent servers creates five budgets. For a stricter shared per-tenant limit, route the key to one authoritative limiter owner or perform refill/consume atomically in a shared store/script with an explicit time/failover policy. Local/regional token allocations can reduce coordination if the product accepts a defined overshoot budget. Do not label a process-local synchronized block globally scalable by itself.

lessonSections.title: Handle failure and key lifecycle
lessonSections.explanation: Choose fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint risk when the limiter store is unavailable; monitor the fallback. Bound key cardinality and idle lifetime in a dynamic registry. Concurrent bucket eviction/recreation must not reset an active budget and grant extra bursts. Backoff retry traffic and test hot tenants so the limiter does not become the bottleneck it was meant to prevent.

walkthroughSteps.title: Resolve trusted tenant
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Look up a configured policy from authenticated identity, not an arbitrary header.

walkthroughSteps.title: Refill with elapsed time
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Add fractional tokens up to capacity under the same lock as consumption.

walkthroughSteps.title: Consume or reject
walkthroughSteps.explanation: Atomically subtract only when sufficient tokens exist; return a clear decision.

walkthroughSteps.title: Choose distributed ownership
walkthroughSteps.explanation: For multiple servers, coordinate the budget and document outage/overshoot behavior.

tradeoffs: The double-based lab is an explanatory local algorithm, not a precision/accounting guarantee for financial quotas. Production designs can use bounded integer/fixed-point accounting and must define clock, failover and TTL semantics.

question: Design a distributed key-value store?
answer: Alice’s service stores `profile:81` and later reads it from another application server. We want a key lookup service with a documented durability and consistency contract. A concurrent Java map is useful inside one node; it cannot by itself keep data across process crashes or coordinate nodes separated by a network.

contentBlocks.text: Design a distributed key-value store: follow one write and one read

Alice’s service stores profile:81 and later reads it from another application server. We want a key lookup service with a documented durability and consistency contract. A concurrent Java map is useful inside one node; it cannot by itself keep data across process crashes or coordinate nodes separated by a network.
All .example names are reserved teaching names. This is an illustrative design, not a claim to implement Raft or any particular database.
1. Choose the contract before drawing replicas

Our starting contract is per-key PUT, GET, DELETE and compare-and-set by version, scoped to an authenticated tenant. We want acknowledged writes to survive the failures covered by the configured quorum and durable storage policy. For this tutorial, linearizable operations for a key are handled by the current leader of its shard; minority partitions cannot accept writes requiring a quorum.

We do not promise cross-shard transactions, unlimited availability during partition, or zero latency. A multi-key operation needs a separately designed transaction/ownership protocol. Atomicity for one key is not automatically a global snapshot.
2. Route the request to the right owner

The operator owns kv.learn.example and configures DNS, load balancing, TLS and workload access. DNS gets the caller to the service; it does not hash individual keys. A router derives the tenant from verified credentials and maps (tenant, key) to a shard using a versioned routing map/hash scheme. Include tenant identity in data, routing, cache and quota boundaries.

For example, the router maps (A, profile:81) to shard S3. S3 has replicas N1, N2 and N3; N1 is currently leader. A stale router gets a controlled ownership redirect/retry rather than being allowed to create an independent writer. Internal nodes authenticate each other as well as client workloads.
3. Define the request and record

PUT /v1/keys/profile%3A81
Authorization: Bearer <tenant-A-workload-credential>
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: change-81

{"value":{"name":"Alice"},"expectedVersion":7}

This illustrative conditional PUT means update only if the authoritative version is 7. The storage record includes tenant, key, value/tombstone, logical version and any defined expiry metadata. Request identity and a result record can make retries recognizable under the service’s retention policy.

Only return that success when the chosen consensus/durable-storage commit contract is met. A failed expected-version comparison returns a conflict such as 409 under this API contract. Authentication and per-key/namespace permission checks happen independently of version matching.
4. Follow the write through the shard
Router, shard leader, replicas and read path

The leader validates the operation, orders it in its replicated log and writes according to the configured durable-log policy. Followers append the replicated entries and acknowledge according to that policy. For a three-voter shard, a majority means two voters. A consensus implementation tracks terms, log matching and the valid commit point; do not replace it with “send to any two servers and accept the newest timestamp.”

After an entry is committed under the consensus protocol, replicas apply the ordered operation to their state machine. Return the successful versioned result at the appropriate point. If compare-and-set requires version 7, it must be evaluated against the authoritative ordered state, so two competing updates cannot both successfully claim the same prior version.
Use an established consensus/storage implementation when building a real service. A few Java methods plus acknowledgements do not implement safe elections, durable recovery or all consensus rules.
5. Follow a read from another client

GET /v1/keys/profile%3A81
Authorization: Bearer <another-authorized-tenant-A-workload>

The router resolves the same shard. For the promised linearizable read, the serving protocol must establish current leadership/read authority, for example through the chosen consensus implementation’s read-index/quorum mechanism, before reading the applied state. Simply asking an old leader or an arbitrary follower can return stale data.

An API may also expose explicitly weaker/stale reads for cheaper local/follower access. Name that choice in the contract. Never silently downgrade a strong read when a quorum is unavailable. A key absent under a completed authoritative read is different from a storage timeout.
6. Crash and retry the same operation

Suppose N1 commits version 8, but the response to Alice disappears. Alice cannot infer failure from timeout. With a stable request identity, the new leader can recognize a retained completed result; a compare-and-set retry with expectedVersion 7 otherwise conflicts because version 8 is already present. Define how the client learns whether its own write succeeded rather than teaching it to blindly overwrite with a new version.

Now stop N1. The remaining voters elect according to the consensus protocol and preserve its committed-log guarantees. An old leader must not continue accepting writes after losing authority; terms and protocol checks fence stale ownership. If fewer than a majority are available, the strong write/read service may be temporarily unavailable. That is the deliberate partition-time consistency trade-off.
7. Recover storage, expiry and deleted records

A node reconstructs its state from a valid snapshot plus later durable log entries. Snapshots/checkpoints must agree with the replicated log position. Retention and compaction must not remove information still needed by lagging replicas or recovery. Durable logs/replicas are not substitutes for tested historical backups against accidental deletion/corruption.

DELETE can be represented as an ordered tombstone until safe cleanup conditions are met. Otherwise a stale replica may resurrect a deleted value. TTL needs a documented clock/expiration contract: replicated expiry decisions and follower read semantics must agree with the promised visibility. Wall clocks across machines are not a universal conflict-resolution oracle.
8. Decide the failure response and authorization boundary

Reject a tenant-A credential trying to read tenant B’s namespace before returning its value or existence where that is sensitive. Access revocation, snapshots, administrative APIs, backups and operational logs all need appropriate authorization. TLS encrypts traffic; it does not decide which caller may modify a key.

If the router is stale, retry the same logical request with bounded attempts against current ownership. If the shard cannot meet the requested guarantee, return a temporary error such as 503, not a fabricated 404 or silent stale success. If a write conflicts by version, report the conflict distinctly from infrastructure failure. Rate-limit hot tenants and bound request/value sizes so one caller cannot exhaust memory or log capacity.
9. Add shards only after one shard is correct

Replication adds copies for one shard’s durability/availability contract. Sharding distributes different keys across ownership groups for scale. If every shard hashes a celebrity key to one group, that hot key still has one authoritative write sequence. More shards do not split a single linearizable key’s writes automatically.

Moving a key range between shards requires a versioned ownership/handoff protocol, transfer/catch-up and fencing so old and new groups cannot both be authoritative. Consistent hashing can reduce remapping but does not supply this protocol. During movement, define retry, read and write behavior explicitly.
10. Walk through acceptance tests

Create version 1, read it through another router, then race two expectedVersion=1 writes and require exactly one successful change under the chosen contract. Lose a reply after commit and retry with the same operation identity. Partition the leader from a majority and ensure it cannot continue acknowledging strong writes. Recover a follower from snapshot/log and verify ordered state. Delete a key, reconnect an old replica and ensure it is not resurrected. Query another tenant’s key and deny it.

These are validation requirements for a real implementation, not claims that this repository runs a distributed store. Measure latency distributions, log/replication lag, disk pressure, leader changes, conflicts and hot-key concentration. Keep backup/restore and failure drills separate from happy-path throughput benchmarks.
References

- [etcd API consistency guarantees](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.5/learning/api_guarantees/)
- [Raft: consensus protocol and paper](https://raft.github.io/)
- [OWASP tenant isolation](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multi_Tenant_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html)

question: Design a notification system with fan-out and retries?
answer: Read in order: each decision below follows from the same real-world situation. Domains ending in .example are reserved teaching names, not live services. These are illustrative designs, not descriptions of a company’s internal implementation.

contentBlocks.text: Build Notification platform: follow the complete user journey

Read in order: each decision below follows from the same real-world situation. Domains ending in .example are reserved teaching names, not live services. These are illustrative designs, not descriptions of a company’s internal implementation.
1. Follow one order confirmation

Order 81 is confirmed and Alice expects an email plus an app notification. The order must remain confirmed even if the email provider is down. “Accepted for sending”, “provider accepted”, “delivered” and “read” are different facts. We therefore record durable notification intent and process delivery asynchronously instead of holding checkout open while every provider responds.
2. Know which domains and credentials do what

The operator configures an HTTPS notification-management API with DNS/TLS. Its workers call approved provider APIs with server-managed credentials. Email also uses an owned sender domain with the provider’s required authentication records such as SPF/DKIM/DMARC configuration; those concern email sender verification, not HTTP user authorization. SMS and mobile push have their own provider credentials and registration rules.
3. Record the business event once

Checkout commits order confirmation and an outbox event together. A relay delivers event e81 to the notification service. The service authenticates the producing workload, checks allowed tenant/event types and records a stable event-recipient-channel identity. A random public caller must not be able to send arbitrary branded messages to arbitrary recipients. Templates and recipient selection belong to trusted business rules.
The concrete API/data vocabulary used in this journey:
POST /notifications with stable event key. Intent(tenant, recipient, template, channel), Preference, DeliveryAttempt(provider ID/status), DedupKey.
A concrete request and observable response for this journey (illustrative API contract):

POST /notifications
Authorization: Bearer <trusted-order-service-credential>
Content-Type: application/json

{"eventId":"e81","orderId":81,"recipientRef":"customer-alice","template":"ORDER_CONFIRMED"}

HTTP/1.1 202 Accepted
{"intentId":"N81","state":"ACCEPTED_FOR_PROCESSING"}

The service resolves authorized tenant/customer contact data and preferences.
202 acknowledges the stored intent; it does not claim the email was delivered.
Repeated e81 for the same permitted recipient/channel resolves to the existing
intent under the documented deduplication policy.
Notification platform component overview
Use this diagram to locate the responsibilities just introduced. Arrows show selected requests/data; the paragraphs distinguish return responses, alternatives and transaction boundaries.
4. Choose channels from preferences

Resolve Alice’s verified contact destinations and current preferences, including necessary transactional versus optional promotional policy. Create channel work with the chosen template version and safe data fields. Do not place full secrets or unnecessary payment/customer details in message bodies or logs. A change of contact address needs verification; a request parameter must not silently redirect sensitive notifications to an attacker.
5. Send and track a delivery attempt

A worker consumes channel work, observes provider rate limits and creates an attempt record. It calls the provider with a stable idempotency key where supported, stores the returned provider reference and handles authenticated status callbacks. Provider accepted means the provider took responsibility under its contract, not proof Alice read the message. Push tokens identify device registrations and can expire.
6. Handle the lost-acknowledgement problem

If the provider accepted an SMS but the worker timed out, retrying may duplicate it. Prefer provider idempotency/status lookup; when unavailable, document the duplicate-versus-loss policy for that channel. Local deduplication cannot make a remote non-idempotent send exactly once. Retry transient errors with bounded backoff and jitter, quarantine permanent failures, and monitor oldest pending intent. A crash after send can cause reprocessing.
7. Expose only authorized status and controls

Alice can inspect her own notification preferences and permitted delivery history. Tenant operators can manage only their authorized templates/recipients; privileged overrides need audit. Unsubscribe/cancellation and queued work must have a defined interaction. If the preference service is unavailable for optional marketing, do not guess consent; apply a safe documented policy.
8. Prove correctness before promotion traffic

Test duplicate e81, a provider timeout, invalid contact, revoked push token, consent change and an unauthorized caller. Preserve order success while workers stop. Then estimate fan-out: one million notifications/hour is about 278/second before channels and retries, but scheduled campaigns produce much larger bursts. Separate channel queues and worker budgets so one failing SMS provider cannot starve all email.
Work the capacity assumption

One million notifications/hour is about 278/second before channel fan-out; a promotion can create a much larger short burst. These are illustrative assumptions; measure the chosen implementation and peak distribution before treating them as capacity.
Explain the journey back

If the provider accepted an SMS but the acknowledgement was lost, what duplicate risk remains? Then explain the hostname, caller identity, object-level permission, authoritative record, success acknowledgement and crash/retry behavior for this same action.

question: Two Sum and its variants?
answer: Return indices of two numbers whose sum equals target. At least two integers; exactly one pair exists. Return zero-based indices in either order; never reuse an index.
explanation: Return indices of two numbers whose sum equals target. At least two integers; exactly one pair exists. Return zero-based indices in either order; never reuse an index.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.

lessonSections.title: Brute force
lessonSections.explanation: Compare every pair of distinct indices. Time O(n²); space O(1).

lessonSections.title: Improved solution and invariant
lessonSections.explanation: Store previously seen values in a map and look up the complement. For [2,7,11,15], store 2 at index 0. At index 1 the complement is 2, so return [0,1]. Look up before inserting to avoid reusing the current index. Time O(n); space O(n).

lessonSections.title: Boundary cases
lessonSections.explanation: [3,3], target=6 → [0,1]; negative values; pair at the end.

lessonSections.title: Variants are different contracts
lessonSections.explanation: One pair of indices uses a complement map; sorted input permits two pointers. For unique value pairs, sort a copy and skip duplicate endpoint values after a match. Counting index pairs instead accumulates prior complement frequency: [1,1,1,1] with target 2 has six index pairs but one unique value pair. Use widened arithmetic for sums/complements. The runnable MockCodingDemo implements all four; a request for all output pairs may require quadratic output size.

question: Merge overlapping intervals?
answer: Merge all overlapping closed intervals. Each closed interval has start <= end. Touching endpoints overlap. Return disjoint merged intervals; empty input is allowed.

lessonSections.explanation: Repeatedly scan all interval pairs and merge any overlap until no pair overlaps. Time O(n³) upper bound; space O(n).

lessonSections.explanation: Sort by start and merge when the next interval overlaps. Sort by start. After [1,3] merges with [2,6], current becomes [1,6]. [8,10] cannot overlap it, so emit current. Sorting guarantees later starts cannot reconnect a finished interval. Time O(n log n); space O(n) output.

question: LRU Cache from scratch?
answer: Use HashMap<K,Node> plus a doubly linked recency list. Every real list node must have one map entry and matching forward/back links. Head is newest and tail is oldest; sentinels handle empty/single-entry boundaries.
explanation: Use HashMap<K,Node> plus a doubly linked recency list. Every real list node must have one map entry and matching forward/back links. Head is newest and tail is oldest; sentinels handle empty/single-entry boundaries.

example: Capacity two: put(1,A), put(2,B), get(1), put(3,C). Key 2 must be evicted.

lessonSections.title: Operations
lessonSections.explanation: get misses without mutation or detaches/moves the found node to newest. put updates and refreshes an existing node; a new entry beyond capacity evicts the tail node from both list and map. Define zero capacity and null behavior explicitly.

lessonSections.title: Complexity and safety
lessonSections.explanation: List work is O(1); hash-table operations are expected/amortized O(1), not a deterministic guarantee under arbitrary collisions. Space is O(capacity). A successful get changes order, so synchronize it with writes for an exact shared local LRU.

lessonSections.title: Solution and tests
lessonSections.explanation: The linked runnable LruCacheDemo includes explicit nodes rather than delegating the implementation to LinkedHashMap. It tests update recency, zero capacity, list/map invariants and 1,000 deterministic operations against an independent access-ordered reference model.

question: Top K frequent elements?
answer: Return the k numbers with the highest occurrence counts. Nonempty integer array; 1 <= k <= distinct values. Assume the top-k set is unique; output order does not matter.
explanation: Return the k numbers with the highest occurrence counts. Nonempty integer array; 1 <= k <= distinct values. Assume the top-k set is unique; output order does not matter.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.

lessonSections.title: Brute force
lessonSections.explanation: For each distinct value, scan the entire input to count it, then repeatedly pick the largest remaining count. Time O(n²); space O(n).

lessonSections.title: Improved solution and invariant
lessonSections.explanation: Count frequencies and maintain a min-heap of size k. Counts are {1:3,2:2,3:1}. A heap capped at k removes the least frequent candidate, retaining 1 and 2 for k=2. Time O(n log k); space O(n).

lessonSections.title: Boundary cases
lessonSections.explanation: k=1; all values equal; k equals distinct count. Heap output is not necessarily sorted.

question: Detect a cycle in a linked list?
answer: Walk the nodes while storing object identities in a set. A repeated node reference reveals the cycle; null ends an acyclic list. Time O(n), extra space O(n). Use reference identity rather than value equality.
explanation: Walk the nodes while storing object identities in a set. A repeated node reference reveals the cycle; null ends an acyclic list. Time O(n), extra space O(n). Use reference identity rather than value equality.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: Nodes A → B → C → B have cycle entry B. Equal node values alone do not mean a cycle.

lessonSections.title: Floyd solution
lessonSections.explanation: Advance slow by one and fast by two. In a finite cycle their relative distance moves by one modulo cycle length and eventually becomes zero. Stop only after checking fast and fast.next for null.

lessonSections.title: Find the entry
lessonSections.explanation: After a meeting, start one pointer at head and advance both by one until they meet at the entry. If the prefix length is mu and cycle length lambda, the meeting-distance relation implies mu steps align their cycle positions. Detection plus entry recovery is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

lessonSections.title: Adversarial tests
lessonSections.explanation: Test null, one node with null next, self-loop, a cycle beginning at head, a nonempty prefix, and distinct nodes with equal values. Never modify next links merely to mark visited nodes.

followups: Prove why the pointers meet inside a cycle.

question: Number of islands?
answer: Count connected groups of land cells in a 2D grid (4-directional adjacency). Rectangular grid contains only 0 water and 1 land. Count components joined horizontally or vertically; diagonal contact does not join islands.
explanation: Count connected groups of land cells in a 2D grid (4-directional adjacency). Rectangular grid contains only 0 water and 1 land. Count components joined horizontally or vertically; diagonal contact does not join islands.

lessonSections.explanation: For every unassigned land cell repeatedly rescan the grid to expand its component until no adjacent land can be added. Time O((rows·cols)²) upper bound; space O(rows·cols).

lessonSections.title: Improved solution and invariant
lessonSections.explanation: Flood-fill each unvisited land cell using an explicit stack. Flood-fill marks land when pushing it, so each cell enters the stack once. answer: Maximize profit from one buy followed by one sell. Non-null array of nonnegative daily prices. Choose at most one buy and a strictly later sell; return zero if no profit exists.

question: Design an ATM?
answer: Separate session authentication, account permission, cash inventory, withdrawal orchestration and hardware adapter. The ATM/controller verifies card/PIN through an appropriate secure banking integration; the lab does not handle real PINs or card data. Derive trusted identity at that boundary rather than treating a passed user string as proof.

The ATM/controller verifies card/PIN through an appropriate secure banking integration; the lab does not handle real PINs or card data. example: Alice withdraws 600 units from notes {500:1, 200:3}; greedy 500 first cannot finish, but three 200 notes can.

lessonSections.title: Domain and transitions
lessonSections.explanation: Model Account/Balance, CashInventory, Withdrawal(requestKey, amount, state) and Dispenser. A real state machine can progress AUTHORIZED → CASH_RESERVED → DISPENSE_REQUESTED → DISPENSED or an explicit UNKNOWN/REVERSED path. Enforce positive amount, limits, funds and an exact feasible denomination plan before decrementing anything.

lessonSections.title: Implement the local decision
lessonSections.explanation: The Java lab uses bounded-note backtracking because a greedy choice can fail for available denominations. Under one local lock it checks owner, idempotency key/payload and balance, finds a plan, then updates balance and inventory together. A duplicate key returns the prior result; a mismatched amount is rejected.

lessonSections.title: Do not confuse local atomicity with dispensing
lessonSections.explanation: A physical dispense can succeed while its reply is lost. Persist a durable operation journal and reconcile device counters/sensor events; do not blindly debit again or instantly reverse while the cash outcome is unknown. A database transaction cannot atomically roll back cash already handed out. Network-bank authorization and local cash reservation need a recovery protocol.

lessonSections.title: Solution limits and tests
lessonSections.explanation: AtmDemo simulates only the local logical decision; it does not operate hardware, persist a ledger or implement banking compliance. It tests non-greedy exact notes, replay, unauthorized subject, conflicting key and no-change failure. Backtracking is exponential in denomination/count choices; bound withdrawal sizes and select an appropriate bounded-change algorithm for a real configuration.

question: Design a stock order book?
answer: This exercise is one instrument, integer price ticks, positive quantities and limit orders with price-time priority. State whether matching uses maker price, how cancellation works and whether market orders/self-trade prevention/auctions exist. The lab deliberately omits those extra market rules.
explanation: This exercise is one instrument, integer price ticks, positive quantities and limit orders with price-time priority. State whether matching uses maker price, how cancellation works and whether market orders/self-trade prevention/auctions exist. The lab deliberately omits those extra market rules.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: S1 sells five units at 100; S2 sells three at 100. B1 buys six with limit 101: fill S1 first for five and S2 for one, at maker price 100.

lessonSections.title: Data structures
lessonSections.explanation: Maintain a buy priority queue ordered by highest price then server sequence and a sell queue ordered by lowest price then sequence. Orders carry stable IDs, immutable original request and mutable remaining quantity. An active-ID map supports cancellation; cancelled heap nodes are lazily skipped. A production price-level book may use ordered price maps plus FIFO queues.

lessonSections.title: Matching operation
lessonSections.explanation: A sequenced submit repeatedly inspects the best opposite order, verifies crossing prices and trades min(takerRemaining,makerRemaining). Update both remaining quantities, remove a finished maker and rest the taker only if quantity remains. Do not reorder same-price makers by client timestamps. The lab serializes commands with synchronized and uses server sequence numbers.

lessonSections.title: Retries and cancellation
lessonSections.explanation: Retain request/result identity so retrying the exact original order ID returns its original submission result without rematching. Reusing the ID with changed parameters conflicts. A cancel applies to the currently resting remainder once; it cannot erase an executed trade. In a real service authenticate clients, bind order ownership and authorize cancellation.

lessonSections.title: Recovery and cost
lessonSections.explanation: The runnable lab tests maker price, same-price FIFO, partial fills, replay, cancellation and payload conflict. It is in-memory, uses lazy tombstones and keeps deduplication history indefinitely, so it is not a production exchange. Journal accepted commands with deterministic sequencing, snapshots/replay and retention in a real design. For t matches, heap work is roughly O((t+1) log n), plus lazy cleanup; cancellation marks O(1) but memory cleanup is deferred.

followups: Which state wins when cancel and execution race?
Why can a retry not simply submit a new order ID?

question: Design a rate limiter class?
answer: Bucket owns capacity, fractional tokens, refill rate, last time and injected monotonic clock. Refill, compare and consume must happen inside one atomic boundary. Limiter selects a configured bucket using trusted caller/tenant identity.

lessonSections.title: Error behavior and scale
lessonSections.explanation: Reject invalid cost/unknown tenant; deny without enough tokens. A controller translates deny to 429 with retry guidance. Independent process-local buckets multiply the effective global limit; use one key owner/shared atomic operation or explicitly allocated local budgets across servers.

question: Design payment processing with idempotent transfers?
answer: Clarify whether this is an internal same-ledger transfer or an external rail. For a same-currency internal transfer, accepted postings must balance, the caller may debit only authorized accounts, and one logical request must not create duplicate postings. Represent currency explicitly and use bounded integer minor units or an appropriate decimal money type, never binary floating-point for ledger amounts.

example: Alice requests transfer T81 of 5,000 paise from authorized account A to account B; the client loses the response after commit.

lessonSections.title: API and data contract
lessonSections.explanation: POST /transfers carries source, destination, amount, currency and a stable idempotency key. Derive actor/tenant from verified credentials, verify debit permission and limits, and bind the key to the operation’s payload fingerprint. Store Transfer, immutable balanced Posting records, account concurrency state and an outbox event. Retain idempotency results under a documented policy.

lessonSections.title: Follow the local transaction
lessonSections.explanation: Claim the scoped key under a unique constraint. Lock/serialize affected account state in a consistent order or use an equivalent guarded transactional design, validate available funds, write balanced postings and update the chosen balance projection with the transfer/result/outbox in one transaction. Retry serialization/deadlock failures within bounds using the same logical identity. A pre-transaction balance read is not sufficient.

lessonSections.title: Handle the lost response
lessonSections.explanation: If commit succeeded, retrying T81 returns the recorded result. Concurrent same-key calls must not both execute the transfer. A different payload with the same key conflicts. If outcome is unknown after timeout, query by operation identity; do not create a fresh key and assume failure.

lessonSections.title: External rails need another protocol
lessonSections.explanation: A remote bank/provider cannot share an ordinary local database commit. Record a pending instruction, deliver through a recoverable outbox/worker, use a stable provider reference and reconcile authenticated confirmations and statement data. Model PENDING/UNKNOWN/CONFIRMED/FAILED explicitly; reversals are new recorded postings, not deletion of history. A webhook or browser return URL alone is not sufficient evidence without its authenticity/state checks.

lessonSections.title: Observe and test
lessonSections.explanation: Test simultaneous retries, competing debits, insufficient funds, crash before/after commit, lost provider acknowledgement and duplicate/out-of-order confirmations. Reconcile ledger versus balance projections and external statements. Monitor unbalanced journals, pending age, duplicate conflicts and reconciliation breaks. Scaling the service must preserve one authoritative account/transfer decision boundary; sharding adds cross-boundary coordination, not free atomicity.

followups: What does successful mean for an internal versus external transfer?
How do you avoid deadlock when two transfers involve the same accounts in reverse order?

question: Design a real-time fraud detection pipeline?
answer: Separate fast authorization-time risk decision from asynchronous investigation/retraining. Decide which events require block, step-up, hold or a documented fallback; availability of a model is not permission to approve every unknown transfer. A risk score is evidence for a policy decision, not an authenticated instruction to move money.

lessonSections.title: Ingest trusted events
lessonSections.explanation: Record stable event ID, tenant/account scope, event and ingestion times, schema version and relevant verified signals. A transactional source outbox prevents a fraud event representing a transfer that never committed where the flow requires committed events.

lessonSections.title: Build and read features
lessonSections.explanation: A stream processor updates windowed velocity/device/account features with explicit late-event and deduplication rules. The decision service reads a versioned feature snapshot, records feature freshness and calls a bounded rules/model evaluation. Keep event-time versus processing-time semantics visible; replaying an event must not double the velocity count.

lessonSections.title: Make a bounded, auditable decision
lessonSections.explanation: Within the endpoint deadline, combine deterministic rules, model/version, available features and policy version into an allow/block/step-up/hold result. Store reason codes and input evidence references that explain the actual decision; do not fabricate a human-readable justification after the fact. Human review and customer-facing messaging have separate access and privacy requirements.

lessonSections.title: Failures, safety and drift
lessonSections.explanation: If model/feature access times out, choose a preapproved conservative rules path, hold/step-up or unavailable result depending on transaction risk. Mark missing/stale features rather than substituting zero silently. Monitor false-positive rates, confirmed fraud, feature lag, model calibration and cohort performance. Delayed labels and adversarial behavior complicate evaluation; raw approval rate alone is insufficient.

lessonSections.title: Validation and scale
lessonSections.explanation: Replay fixed historical/test event sequences with deduplication, late data and stale features. Test endpoint deadlines, tenant isolation, replay determinism for recorded versions and malformed producer events. Partition feature updates by a key appropriate to the rule, recognizing that cross-account/device aggregation may require another stage. Keep an asynchronous investigation/retraining pipeline from becoming a synchronous dependency for every transfer.

Which decision artifacts let an investigator reproduce the applied policy?

question: Design trade settlement and reconciliation?
answer: An order-book fill is not proof assets and cash have settled. Record executed trade identity and contractual obligations, relevant parties, instrument/currency, amounts, lifecycle and business-date/calendar semantics. Settlement timing and rules vary by market; clarify them rather than assume one global schedule.

lessonSections.title: Create durable obligations
lessonSections.explanation: Consume authenticated execution events with stable trade IDs; deduplicate and validate them, create versioned obligations and outbox instructions transactionally. Apply reference data and configured calendars/cutoffs using explicit time zones. Keep amendments/cancellations as versioned events with allowed transitions instead of overwriting the original evidence.

lessonSections.title: Process external instructions
lessonSections.explanation: Workers submit instructions to the chosen custodian/clearing/settlement infrastructure with stable references. Authenticate and deduplicate confirmations. Model pending, matched, settled, failed and unknown states according to that rail’s contract. A timeout is not proof of rejection; reconcile before resending in a way that could duplicate settlement.

lessonSections.title: Reconcile three views
lessonSections.explanation: Compare internal trade/obligation/ledger state, external confirmations and authoritative statements/positions using declared identifiers, amounts, currency, value date and version. Classify missing, duplicate, quantity/amount and timing breaks. Do not fuzzy-match ambiguous records into an automatic clean status merely to make totals agree.

lessonSections.title: Resolve breaks with controls
lessonSections.explanation: Create a durable case with evidence and assigned owner. Automated safe retries and authorized manual repair require explicit policy, audit and appropriate separation of duties. Use adjustment/reversal records rather than deleting history. Late statements should update reconciliation state idempotently and may reopen a previously provisional comparison.

lessonSections.title: Test recovery and reporting
lessonSections.explanation: Test duplicate instructions/confirmations, partial settlement where supported, calendar boundaries, late files, mismatched currency, ambiguous matches and restart during a batch. Version input files and reconciliation rules; checkpoint progress with sink idempotency. Report pending age, unreconciled exposure and break counts without labeling a matched instruction as finally settled unless the evidence supports it.

question: Design an audit log that cannot be tampered with?
answer: Define the attacker and trust boundaries. No ordinary application table is absolutely tamper-proof against every administrator and compromised key. Aim for append-only access controls, independently verifiable tamper evidence, protected retention and monitored custody. Explain exactly which principals and failure modes the design resists.

Aim for append-only access controls, independently verifiable tamper evidence, protected retention and monitored custody. Explain exactly which principals and failure modes the design resists.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: A privileged operator tries to modify or delete an earlier payment event and conceal that change.

lessonSections.title: Record structured facts
lessonSections.explanation: Capture stable event ID, actor/workload identity, tenant, action, target, before/after references where appropriate, outcome, correlation ID, timestamp and schema/version. Avoid copying secrets or unnecessary personal data. Bind business-state changes and audit intent using a transactional outbox where possible; audit omissions also matter.

lessonSections.title: Make modification detectable
lessonSections.explanation: An ordered stream can hash each canonically encoded event with the prior hash and sequence. Sign/anchor checkpoints in an independently controlled destination so rewriting an entire local chain or truncating its tail is detectable. Protect signing keys, rotate with verification metadata and define clock/ordering semantics. A hash chain alone does not stop an attacker who can rewrite all records and all anchors.

lessonSections.title: Protect retention and access
lessonSections.explanation: Write protected object versions to an appropriate WORM/retention store with separate writer, reader and retention-administration privileges. Choose retention/hold rules with the responsible compliance team. For example, object-lock protections apply to specified object versions; a new object version/delete marker does not mean the protected version changed. Governance versus stricter retention modes have different bypass behavior.

lessonSections.title: Verify and investigate
lessonSections.explanation: Run independent sequence/checkpoint/hash/signature verification, alert on gaps and failed writes, and keep redundant custody/backups. Auditors query an authorized index while verifying evidence against the protected source; rebuilding a search index must not rewrite original history. Access to the audit service itself is audited through a separate appropriate boundary.

lessonSections.title: Failure and acceptance tests
lessonSections.explanation: Test attempted overwrite/delete, missing sequence, altered payload, chain rewrite without anchor authority, truncated tail, key rotation, clock anomalies and an unavailable archive. Decide which sensitive business operations must fail or durably buffer if required audit capture cannot be guaranteed. Do not return compliance assurances based solely on using a named storage product.

question: HashMap internals and what changed in Java 8?
answer: A HashMap uses hash spreading to choose a bucket, then checks hash and equals among entries. Equal keys must have equal hashCode; unequal keys may collide. Power-of-two table capacity allows a bit-mask index. Resizing redistributes bins as capacity grows; default load factor is a sizing policy, not a guarantee of constant latency.
explanation: A HashMap uses hash spreading to choose a bucket, then checks hash and equals among entries. Equal keys must have equal hashCode; unequal keys may collide. Power-of-two table capacity allows a bit-mask index. Resizing redistributes bins as capacity grows; default load factor is a sizing policy, not a guarantee of constant latency.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: Many distinct keys collide in one bucket, and a mutable key is changed after insertion.

lessonSections.title: Java 8 change
lessonSections.explanation: OpenJDK HashMap can convert a heavily populated collision bin into a balanced tree when thresholds and minimum table capacity permit. Common OpenJDK constants are treeify threshold 8 and minimum table capacity 64; below that it may resize rather than treeify. These are implementation details, not a universal Map contract. Tree-bin tie breaking/comparability details matter; do not promise identical asymptotic guarantees for every pathological key type.

lessonSections.title: Practical mistakes
lessonSections.explanation: Changing fields used by equals/hashCode after insertion can make lookup fail even though iteration still shows the entry. HashMap is not thread-safe; fail-fast iteration is best effort, not a concurrency control. Null handling differs from ConcurrentHashMap. To safely accumulate concurrently, use documented atomic concurrent-map operations rather than synchronized-looking combinations of get and put.

lessonSections.title: Explain and test
lessonSections.explanation: Demonstrate two equal key instances retrieving one mapping, distinct colliding keys retaining separate values, resizing with stable keys and a mutable-key lookup failure. Explain expected/amortized behavior and why poorly distributed hashes and unnecessary resizing hurt. The LLD striped-map lab makes collisions, MIN_VALUE hashing and atomic updates explicit without pretending to be OpenJDK internals.

followups: When does a bin resize rather than treeify?
Why does a mutable hash key break lookup even without removal?

question: How does @Transactional work, and when does it silently fail??
answer: In Spring’s typical proxy mode, a call entering through a configured transactional proxy is intercepted. The selected transaction manager starts or joins the resource transaction according to propagation/isolation settings, invokes the method and completes commit/rollback according to outcome and rules. The annotation itself is metadata; it is not a Java keyword that wraps every call.
explanation: In Spring’s typical proxy mode, a call entering through a configured transactional proxy is intercepted. The selected transaction manager starts or joins the resource transaction according to propagation/isolation settings, invokes the method and completes commit/rollback according to outcome and rules. The annotation itself is metadata; it is not a Java keyword that wraps every call.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: A service calls this.transfer() internally and expects the annotation on transfer to start a transaction.

lessonSections.title: Common no-advice boundaries
lessonSections.explanation: Self-invocation through this bypasses proxy advice in the usual proxy mode. Manually constructed objects are not automatically managed/advised. Private methods cannot be advised through ordinary proxy interception, and final/class/method and visibility rules depend on the proxy mechanism and framework setup. State the actual configuration rather than claiming every non-public method always behaves identically.

lessonSections.title: Rollback surprises
lessonSections.explanation: Default Spring rollback rules normally roll back on unchecked exceptions/Error, while checked exceptions require appropriate configuration unless configured defaults differ. Swallowing an exception may make the interceptor see normal completion, though a participating operation may already have marked rollback-only. An outer transaction can then fail at commit rather than silently succeed. readOnly is not a universal write prohibition.

lessonSections.title: Resource/thread limits
lessonSections.explanation: Thread-bound imperative transactions do not automatically propagate to a new executor thread. Reactive transactions have different context rules. A local database transaction does not include an HTTP payment call or another unrelated transaction manager. Holding database locks while waiting on remote I/O increases risk and does not make the remote effect atomic.

lessonSections.title: Fix and verify
lessonSections.explanation: Move the transactional use case to an injected service entered through its proxy, or use an appropriate programmatic boundary when justified. Define propagation/rollback deliberately. Use integration tests against the real database and failure path, checking final committed rows from outside the test’s own transaction so a test rollback cannot hide an error.

followups: How can a caught exception still result in UnexpectedRollbackException?
Why does a test annotated @Transactional sometimes hide a missing production boundary?

question: synchronized vs ReentrantLock?
answer: Both provide mutual exclusion and the required visibility/ordering relationship for properly protected shared state. Both are reentrant for the owning thread. Neither fixes lock-order deadlock or a workflow that reads state outside the protected boundary; neither coordinates separate JVMs.
explanation: Both provide mutual exclusion and the required visibility/ordering relationship for properly protected shared state. Both are reentrant for the owning thread. Neither fixes lock-order deadlock or a workflow that reads state outside the protected boundary; neither coordinates separate JVMs.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: Two threads update a shared local invariant; another operation needs a timed wait for a lock.

lessonSections.title: Choose deliberately
lessonSections.explanation: synchronized offers structured intrinsic-monitor acquisition/release when entering/leaving a block, including exceptional exits. ReentrantLock adds tryLock, timed/interruptible acquisition, optional fairness and multiple Condition queues. Explicit locks must be released in finally, and unlock only after acquisition succeeded.

lessonSections.title: Wait and signal correctly
lessonSections.explanation: wait/notify belong to an owned intrinsic monitor; Condition await/signal belong to the matching held Lock. Recheck predicates in a loop because wakeups do not guarantee the desired state still holds. Fairness can trade throughput for an ordering policy and does not guarantee arbitrary application progress.

lessonSections.title: Virtual-thread version caveat
lessonSections.explanation: On Java 21, blocking while holding synchronized can pin a carrier. JDK 24 changed monitor-related pinning through JEP 491. Do not replace every synchronized block based on an outdated universal warning; state the target runtime, keep critical sections short and measure contention. Native/foreign behavior and other resource limits still require analysis.
