answer: A system prompt explains intended behavior but cannot be the only confidentiality control. The API/tool layer must authorize against verified identity and object scope. If Alice’s tool can only query her permitted accounts, the text all transactions does not widen that authority.
explanation: A system prompt explains intended behavior but cannot be the only confidentiality control. The API/tool layer must authorize against verified identity and object scope. If Alice’s tool can only query her permitted accounts, the text all transactions does not widen that authority.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: Assume prompts can be manipulated; preserve the authorization boundary even if the model follows the malicious request.

lessonSections.title: Layered controls
lessonSections.explanation: Use narrow tool schemas, validate parameters, bind trusted context outside model-controlled fields, and isolate untrusted retrieved/user content from instructions. Restrict tool/network credentials and avoid arbitrary SQL or generic internal fetch tools. Apply bounded result sizes and appropriate monitoring.

lessonSections.title: Demonstrate denial
lessonSections.explanation: Run the exact attack, encoded/paraphrased variants and injection inside a retrieved document. Even if the model requests Bob’s account, the tool returns a permitted denial and no Bob records enter the prompt. Log the denial safely; do not expose protected content inside an error message.

lessonSections.title: Be honest about residual risk
lessonSections.explanation: No prompt-injection filter guarantees universal model obedience. The security objective is that compromised model behavior cannot bypass independent data/action authorization. Review indirect leakage through summaries, citations, timing, logs and cached conversation state as well.

followups: How would the design behave if the model completely ignored the system prompt?
Can a retrieval filter applied only after generation protect data already sent to the model?

question: Make LLM output auditable when asked why an answer was given?
answer: Use a correlation ID tying actor/tenant authorization, request time, prompt/template version, requested and resolved model/deployment/version where available, generation parameters, tool names/arguments/results or approved evidence references, retrieval document versions and final response together.
explanation: Use a correlation ID tying actor/tenant authorization, request time, prompt/template version, requested and resolved model/deployment/version where available, generation parameters, tool names/arguments/results or approved evidence references, retrieval document versions and final response together.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: An authorized reviewer needs to trace a specific account-assistant response without exposing unrelated customer data.

lessonSections.title: Preserve evidence safely
lessonSections.explanation: Store necessary audit artifacts with encryption, role-based access, retention/redaction and integrity controls. Hashes can help verify evidence identity but cannot reconstruct deleted content; decide which permitted source snapshots/references must remain available for the audit purpose. Do not indiscriminately log secrets or full account data.

lessonSections.title: Explain evidence, not private reasoning
lessonSections.explanation: Provide permitted source citations, tool outputs and policy/authorization decisions that support the final answer. Do not promise access to hidden model chain-of-thought or fabricate a post-hoc rationale as historical truth. An audit trail is evidence of the pipeline, not proof the model internally reasoned exactly as a generated explanation says.

lessonSections.title: Account for reproducibility limits
lessonSections.explanation: Model nondeterminism, provider aliases and unavailable historical versions can prevent bit-for-bit regeneration. Pin/version what you can, retain actual output and evidence, and distinguish replaying recorded decisions from re-querying today’s model. Test retrieval/version continuity and evidence access for an auditor.

followups: What must be retained if the source policy later changes?
Why is a model-generated explanation not sufficient historical evidence?

question: Your LLM provider times out at peak: what is the fallback??
answer: Apply an end-to-end deadline, bounded concurrency/queue, circuit breaker and tightly bounded retries with jitter where appropriate. Do not let every layer multiply retries. Cancellation may not stop provider-side work, so also track cost and orphaned requests.
explanation: Apply an end-to-end deadline, bounded concurrency/queue, circuit breaker and tightly bounded retries with jitter where appropriate. Do not let every layer multiply retries. Cancellation may not stop provider-side work, so also track cost and orphaned requests.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: A customer asks for an account balance while the model endpoint is slow.

lessonSections.title: Choose a safe product fallback
lessonSections.explanation: For account facts, use a deterministic authorized account-service response or a clearly unavailable/try-again path; do not invent a balance. For general FAQs, use a versioned approved static answer when appropriate. Financial actions remain unavailable unless their independent authorized workflow can safely proceed without the model.

lessonSections.title: Treat a second provider as a separate deployment decision
lessonSections.explanation: Fallback to another model/provider requires approved data handling, credential scope, residency/retention and quality evaluation, not an ad-hoc endpoint swap. Revalidate output behavior and tool constraints. A stale cached answer must be identity-scoped and permitted by a freshness policy; yesterday’s balance may be unacceptable.

lessonSections.title: Test overload behavior
lessonSections.explanation: Simulate slow responses, partial tool success, reconnect/retry and failover. Monitor user-visible latency, errors, fallback usage, queue age and correctness separately. Explain what the user sees and which operations are deliberately refused.

followups: Why is a cached previous balance an unsafe universal fallback?
How do you stop a retry storm from making the outage worse?

question: Answer quality dropped with zero code changes: what changed??
answer: Confirm the regression using a fixed, versioned evaluation set and real authorized cohorts. Separate retrieval failures, tool/data failures, generation errors and evaluation changes. A changed customer mix or label pipeline can look like a model regression.
explanation: Confirm the regression using a fixed, versioned evaluation set and real authorized cohorts. Separate retrieval failures, tool/data failures, generation errors and evaluation changes. A changed customer mix or label pipeline can look like a model regression.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: A stable application release suddenly gives worse answers on the same product area.

lessonSections.title: Inspect non-code dependencies
lessonSections.explanation: Check resolved model/deployment versions and moving aliases, prompt/config/feature-flag changes, retrieval corpus/index/chunking/embedding versions, ACL/tenant filtering, source freshness, tool schemas and API data. Check token/truncation budgets, provider routing/parameters and load-induced timeout/fallback rates. These are hypotheses to investigate, not assumed causes.

lessonSections.title: Compare controlled snapshots
lessonSections.explanation: Compare last-good and current evidence under the same inputs; replay recorded tool/retrieval results to isolate generation and independently test retrieval recall. Track citations/faithfulness and refusal/error rates, not only a single average score. Redact/protect customer examples in the investigation.

lessonSections.title: Recover and prevent recurrence
lessonSections.explanation: Roll back the identified version/config/index where safe, or use an approved fallback. Pin/version dependencies when possible and record resolved versions when not. Add canary evals and change alerts across the whole pipeline. Communicate the observed cause, scope and evidence instead of saying the model got moody.

followups: What artifact lets you distinguish a corpus change from a model change?
Why can a permission fix reduce recall without being a regression?

question: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a risky change?
answer: Describe the actual change, your responsibility and the specific customer/business invariant at risk. State what you knew then and what was uncertain. Avoid disclosing confidential customer details.
explanation: Describe the actual change, your responsibility and the specific customer/business invariant at risk. State what you knew then and what was uncertain. Avoid disclosing confidential customer details.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: Use a real event from your work; the structure below is a template, not a fabricated personal story.

lessonSections.title: Action with evidence
lessonSections.explanation: Explain how you tested or demonstrated the risk, who you involved and the concrete alternative you proposed. For example, an actual retry/idempotency concern should be supported by the real failure experiment or review finding, not a hypothetical claim presented as history.

lessonSections.title: Decision and outcome
lessonSections.explanation: Describe how the decision was made, what shipped or changed, and the observed result. Use only real measurements; if an incident was avoided, do not pretend you can measure a counterfactual loss precisely. Credit collaborators and own any mistake in your own analysis.

lessonSections.title: Reflection
lessonSections.explanation: Explain what you would repeat or improve: earlier invariants, smaller rollout, better failure tests or escalation timing. A strong answer shows constructive disagreement and accountability, not that you always won the argument.

followups: What evidence changed someone’s mind?
What would you do if the owner accepted the risk anyway?

question: Describe a production incident you owned end to end?
answer: Give the observed customer impact, detection signal and your role. Explain what was known at each stage rather than narrating with hindsight. State actual duration/scope only if you can substantiate it.
explanation: Give the observed customer impact, detection signal and your role. Explain what was known at each stage rather than narrating with hindsight. State actual duration/scope only if you can substantiate it.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: Choose an incident you actually handled and clearly distinguish your work from the team’s.

lessonSections.title: Contain before speculating
lessonSections.explanation: Describe triage, ownership, communications and the reversible containment/rollback decision. Explain how you preserved evidence and avoided risky fixes while uncertain. Customer updates should separate confirmed facts from hypotheses.

lessonSections.title: Recover and verify
lessonSections.explanation: Explain the fix or rollback, data reconciliation if applicable and how you verified the real user journey recovered. A green dashboard or restarted process alone may not prove correctness. Mention follow-up on stuck/duplicate operations if that happened in your real incident.

lessonSections.title: Learn and close
lessonSections.explanation: Summarize contributing causes without blame, concrete owners/actions, and how their effectiveness was checked. Be candid about decisions you would change and avoid claiming sole credit for a coordinated response.

followups: How did you know recovery was correct, not merely available?
Which follow-up action actually changed the next incident outcome?

question: How do you balance speed with compliance requirements??
answer: Identify the actual delivery goal, data/action risk, mandatory controls and accountable policy owners. Separate hard requirements from a process habit that can be improved. Do not give legal interpretations beyond your role.
explanation: Identify the actual delivery goal, data/action risk, mandatory controls and accountable policy owners. Separate hard requirements from a process habit that can be improved. Do not give legal interpretations beyond your role.
why: Attempt the question before reading the model answer. Explain assumptions, invariants, trade-offs and evidence in your own words.
example: Answer through a real delivery decision and your organization’s actual controls, not a promise to bypass requirements.

lessonSections.title: Move fast within safe boundaries
lessonSections.explanation: Offer a smaller scope, staged rollout, read-only release, synthetic-data prototype or automated evidence/test path that preserves required controls. Involve security/compliance reviewers early enough to change the design rather than ask for a rubber stamp at the end.

lessonSections.title: Make the decision reviewable
lessonSections.explanation: Record the control mapping, test evidence, residual risk, approvals required by policy and rollback/operating plan. A deadline or an AI recommendation does not itself authorize an exception. Escalate a genuine unresolved conflict to the accountable owner.

lessonSections.title: Use an honest outcome
lessonSections.explanation: Describe what your real team delivered, what was deferred, the actual customer/control result and what process improvement carried forward. The lesson should show proportionate rigor and good judgment, not speed versus safety as a false binary.

followups: Which part of the process did you automate without weakening the control?
What would you refuse to trade away for the deadline?
